facts.claim: China's VAT Law, in force from 1 January 2026, sets VAT at 6% for services and intangibles not listed at 13% (goods, repair, movable-property leasing), 9% (transport, postal, basic telecoms, construction, real-estate leasing, listed goods) or zero (Art. 10); hotel accommodation is not among the services listed at 13% or 9%. The State Taxation Administration's 2019 Q&A puts lifestyle services at 6%, and a Fujian finance department page quoting the 2016 notice lists catering and accommodation within lifestyle services. EDITOR: the rate for hotel rooms is our reading of these texts, not a sentence in any one of them.

facts.claim: Art. 7 of the VAT Law says VAT is a tax outside the price (the sales amount excludes VAT) and must be shown separately on the transaction document; Art. 16 of the implementing regulation sets out how to compute the sales amount when the seller prices tax-inclusive (tax-inclusive amount divided by 1 plus the rate).

facts.claim: Our arithmetic, not an official rate: a room quoted at 1,000 yuan, with VAT assumed to apply to the room and any service charge together, costs 1,000 yuan if VAT and the charge are included, 1,100 yuan if VAT is included but a 10% charge is not, and 1,166 yuan (1,000 x 1.10 x 1.06) if both a 10% charge and 6% VAT are added; a 15% charge would add 150 yuan instead of 100.

facts.claim: Shanghai's official guidance says foreign guests staying in hotels present a valid passport or residence permit and fill in a temporary accommodation registration form (source: Shanghai Municipal Bureau of Public Security). The NIA says that under Article 39 of the Exit and Entry Administration Law hotels register foreign guests' stays and send the information to the local public security organ; the Ministry of Public Security's rules require the form to reach the police within 24 hours, and in May 2024 the authorities said hotels must not refuse foreign guests because they lack the capacity to process the paperwork (China Daily, hosted on the Shanghai government site).
